L13-a49183: Excision and primary anastomosis (EPA) removes a short stricture and joins healthy urethral ends without tension. Selection depends on stricture site, length, fibrosis and the risk of penile shortening. Current EAU guidance favors transecting EPA for short, nearly obliterative post-traumatic bulbar strictures with full-thickness fibrosis, and non-transecting EPA or a free graft for short bulbar strictures without straddle injury. <sup>[[16]](#ref16)</sup>
L15-d9d361: For graft-based alternatives in longer strictures, see [Buccal Mucosa Graft](/docs/foundations/surgical-principles/grafts/buccal-mucosa). For the vessel-sparing modification, see [Jordan Vessel-Sparing EPA](/docs/surgical-techniques/04a-urethral-reconstruction/jordan-vessel-sparing-epa) and [Non-Transecting Bulbar Urethroplasty](/docs/surgical-techniques/04a-urethral-reconstruction/non-transecting-bulbar). For pelvic-fracture posterior urethral injury, see [Pelvic Fracture Urethral Injury (PFUI)](/docs/special-populations/05a-trauma-emergencies/pfui). The clinical condition is at [Urethral Stricture](/docs/clinical-conditions/03b-voiding-outlet/urethral-stricture).

L38-e1ecc4: The procedure is performed via a perineal approach with the patient in lithotomy position:
L40-4dee85: 1. **Exposure**. Midline perineal incision; bulbospongiosus muscle divided to expose the bulbar urethra.
L41-6abd0a: 2. **Identification**. Strictured segment identified, aided by preoperative retrograde urethrography and intraoperative assessment (calibration, cystoscopy).
L42-441b42: 3. **Excision**. Fibrotic segment excised back to healthy, well-vascularized urethral tissue on both ends.
L43-b52c1b: 4. **Spatulation**. Both urethral ends spatulated on opposite sides (typically dorsal and ventral) to widen the anastomotic lumen and prevent circumferential scar contracture.
L44-f816ab: 5. **Mobilization**. Urethra mobilized to permit a tension-free anastomosis. Avoid excessive mobilization or forced approximation. Elaborated perineal maneuvers such as inferior pubectomy or supracrural rerouting belong to selected complex posterior or PFUI reconstructions, not routine anterior bulbar EPA.
L45-2ce260: 6. **Anastomosis**. Tension-free, mucosa-to-mucosa anastomosis using absorbable sutures (typically 4-0 or 5-0 polyglycolic acid), interrupted or running.
L46-a68abb: 7. **Catheter**. Urethral catheter (16–18 Fr) left in place, with duration tailored to the repair. Assess extravasation by urethrography before removal; selected uncomplicated short repairs can have earlier removal. EAU notes an indwelling catheter is commonly left two to three weeks, with extravasation of 2.2-11.5% at three weeks; after uncomplicated anterior EPA, removal at one versus two weeks gave similar extravasation (6.8% versus 4.5%) and recurrence (4.9% versus 5.2%) in one study. <sup>[[17]](#ref17)</sup>
L52-47e538: A major evolution in technique has been the introduction of **vessel-sparing (non-transecting) EPA (VS-EPA)**, first described in 2007.<sup>[[9]](#ref9)</sup> Non-transecting EPA preserves the bulbar arteries and the dorsal vascular supply of the corpus spongiosum, theoretically reducing the risk of erectile dysfunction and glans ischemia.

L114-348da0: **EPAPP** is a novel technique designed to extend the applicability of anastomotic urethroplasty to longer bulbar strictures that would traditionally require grafting or flap reconstruction. Described by VanDyke, Baumgarten, and Ortiz in 2021, the innovation is the addition of ventral corporal body plication, which shortens the distance between the two healthy urethral ends and enables a tension-free primary anastomosis without graft material.<sup>[[15]](#ref15)</sup>
L118-161cb4: After excision of the strictured segment, plication sutures are placed on the ventral surface of the corpora cavernosa to reduce the gap between the proximal and distal urethral stumps. This effectively "telescopes" the corporal bodies, allowing direct mucosa-to-mucosa reanastomosis even when the gap would otherwise be too large for standard EPA. EPAPP is positioned as an alternative to perineal urethrostomy for patients with long or complex bulbar strictures who may not be ideal candidates for grafting.<sup>[[15]](#ref15)</sup>

L153-c1c01d: The corporal plication used in EPAPP is mechanically similar to but conceptually distinct from the tunical plication performed for Peyronie's disease. In Peyronie's surgery, plication is applied to the convex side of the tunica albuginea to shorten it and correct curvature. In EPAPP, plication is ventral and serves to reduce corporal length to bridge a urethral gap; it does not correct curvature. The mechanical principle of shortening tissue through plication sutures is shared. See [Peyronie's Correction](/docs/surgical-techniques/04e-genital-reconstruction/genital-reconstruction-principles) for the Peyronie's-specific application.
